questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — During a secondary-school biology lab, two heterozygous parents (Aa × Aa) are crossed. What are the offspring genotype and phenotype ratios?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 : 2 : 1 (genotype AA : Aa : aa) and 3 : 1 (phenotype dominant : recessive)

options.label: C
options.text: All dominant

questions.explanation: Monohybrid cross Aa × Aa gives offspring genotype ratio 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, and phenotype ratio 3 dominant (A_) : 1 recessive (aa).

questions.questionText: Scenario #2 — During a secondary-school biology lab, according to the 10% rule in ecosystems, what fraction of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy increases at higher trophic levels

options.label: B
options.text: 100% of energy is transferred

options.label: C
options.text: Approximately 10% of energy is passed from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat, in undigested matter, or used in respiration

options.label: D
options.text: All energy passes to decomposers only

questions.explanation: Energy flow in ecosystems: about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (10% rule). The rest is lost as heat (respiration), in undigested waste, or used for life processes. This is why food chains typically have only 4–5 trophic levels.

questions.questionText: Scenario #3 — During a secondary-school biology lab, a test cross is performed between a heterozygous parent (Aa) and a homozygous recessive (aa). What fraction of the offspring will be heterozygous?

options.label: A
options.text: All offspring are heterozygous (Aa)

options.label: B
options.text: 25% heterozygous (Aa) and 75% homozygous recessive (aa)

options.label: C
options.text: 75% homozygous dominant (AA)

options.label: D
options.text: 50% heterozygous (Aa) and 50% homozygous recessive (aa)

questions.explanation: Cross Aa × aa (test cross): parental gametes (A, a) × (a) → offspring Aa, Aa, aa, aa. Probability of heterozygous Aa = 1/2 (50%); probability of homozygous aa = 1/2 (50%).

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes eutrophication in a freshwater lake?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess nitrates and phosphates (from fertilisers/sewage) cause algal blooms; algae die and decompose by aerobic bacteria, depleting oxygen and killing aquatic life

options.label: B
options.text: Eutrophication is caused by adding oxygen to lakes

options.label: C
options.text: Eutrophication means fish become larger

options.label: D
options.text: Eutrophication only happens in the ocean

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — During a secondary-school biology lab, where is the hormone adrenaline produced in the human body?

options.text: Thyroid gland (in the neck)

options.label: B
options.text: Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)

options.label: C
options.text: Adrenal glands (situated above the kidneys)

options.label: D

questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is produced by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of each kidney. It increases heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose in 'fight or flight' situations.

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes Mendel's Law of Segregation?

options.label: A
options.text: Law of segregation: each individual has two alleles for a trait which separate during gamete formation; each gamete carries only one allele

options.label: B
options.text: All traits are determined by one allele only

options.label: C
options.text: Genes cannot be inherited from parents

options.label: D
options.text: All alleles always stay together in gametes

questions.explanation: Mendel's First Law (Law of Segregation): every individual possesses two alleles for each trait, and these alleles separate (segregate) during gamete formation so each gamete carries only one allele. The zygote restores the pair at fertilisation.

options.label: D
options.text: Only plants can be cloned

questions.explanation: Cloning: producing genetically identical organisms from a single parent. Examples: asexual reproduction (binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation); somatic cell nuclear transfer (e.g., Dolly the sheep); tissue culture (plant cuttings in lab).

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly distinguishes continuous variation from discontinuous variation?

options.label: A
options.text: Continuous variation shows a range of phenotypes (e.g., height, weight); discontinuous variation shows distinct categories (e.g., blood group, tongue-rolling)

options.label: B
options.text: Continuous variation has distinct categories

options.label: C
options.text: Both types only depend on environment

options.label: D
options.text: Discontinuous variation is influenced by many genes

questions.explanation: Continuous variation: a range of phenotypes with no discrete categories (influenced by many genes + environment); examples: height, weight, skin colour, leaf length. Discontinuous variation: discrete categories (one or few genes); examples: ABO blood group, tongue-rolling ability, seed shape, presence/absence of dimples.

questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA technology: cutting DNA from two different organisms with restriction enzymes, joining them with DNA ligase, and inserting the recombinant DNA into a host cell (e.g., bacteria) to produce useful proteins (e.g., human insulin, growth hormone).

questions.explanation: Sex-linked traits (X-linked recessive) such as haemophilia and colour blindness: heterozygous females (X^H X^h) are carriers (phenotypically normal but carry one allele); males (X^h Y) express the trait. Cross X^H X^h × X^H Y → 1/4 X^h Y (affected male).

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, how does antibiotic resistance develop in bacterial populations?

options.label: A
options.text: All bacteria develop resistance after one exposure to antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: Bacteria become resistant by becoming larger

options.label: C
options.text: Resistance is caused by drinking antibiotics

options.label: D
options.text: Some bacteria have natural resistance; antibiotics kill susceptible ones; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly describes codominance?

options.label: C
options.text: All codominant alleles produce recessive phenotypes

options.label: D
options.text: Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (e.g., ABO blood group AB, where both A and B antigens are present)

questions.explanation: Codominance: both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (no dominant/recessive relationship). Example: ABO blood groups — IAIA = A, IBIB = B, IAIB = AB (both A and B antigens expressed). This is different from incomplete dominance, where traits blend.

questions.questionText: Scenario #15 — While observing pond water under a microscope, what is the correct sequence of events in a reflex arc?

questions.explanation: A reflex arc follows: stimulus → receptor (detects) → sensory neurone → (relay neurone in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector (muscle/gland) → response. This pathway is involuntary and rapid.

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — In a mangrove swamp study, what is the correct sequence of stages in ecological succession?

Each stage modifies the environment, allowing the next community to develop.

questions.questionText: Scenario #11 — In a mangrove swamp study, which of the following correctly compares Darwin's and Lamarck's theories of evolution?

questions.explanation: Darwin's natural selection: individuals with favourable variations (arising randomly) survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest); over generations, the favourable trait accumulates in the population. questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a mangrove swamp study, how does antibiotic resistance develop in bacterial populations?

options.text: Some bacteria have natural resistance; antibiotics kill susceptible ones; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring

options.label: D
options.text: Resistance is caused by drinking antibiotics

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.questionText: Scenario #15 — In a mangrove swamp study, what are the sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms?

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — At a national park visitor centre, which of the following correctly distinguishes continuous variation from discontinuous variation?

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — In a school garden experiment, which of the following correctly describes Mendel's Law of Segregation?

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — In a school garden experiment, which of the following correctly compares Darwin's and Lamarck's theories of evolution?

options.text: Lamarck proposed natural selection; Darwin proposed inheritance of acquired characteristics

options.label: B
options.text: Both Darwin and Lamarck proposed identical theories

options.label: C
options.text: Darwin's theory of natural selection states that organisms with favourable variations survive and reproduce; Lamarck's theory (now rejected) stated that acquired characteristics during life could be passed to offspring

options.label: D
options.text: Darwin's theory was based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics

questions.explanation: Darwin's natural selection: individuals with favourable variations (arising randomly) survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest); over generations, the favourable trait accumulates in the population. Lamarck's (rejected) inheritance of acquired characteristics: features developed during life (e.g., giraffe's long neck from stretching) are passed to offspring.

questions.explanation: Genetically modified (GM) foods: contain one or more genes transferred from another species, conferring desirable traits (e.g., Bt corn with bacterial Bt gene for pest resistance; golden rice with added β-carotene for vitamin A). Controversies: unknown long-term health effects, environmental risks, ethical concerns.

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — During a marine biology field study, what are the sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms?

questions.explanation: Continuous variation: a range of phenotypes with no discrete categories (influenced by many genes + environment); examples: height, weight, skin colour, leaf length. Discontinuous variation: discrete categories (one or few genes); examples: ABO blood group, tongue-rolling ability, seed shape, presence/absence of dimples.

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — In a vaccination programme, what is the correct sequence of stages in ecological succession?

options.label: A
options.text: All stages occur simultaneously

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: Pioneer community → Intermediate community → Climax community

options.label: D
options.text: Climax community → Pioneer community → Intermediate

questions.explanation: Ecological succession on bare ground (e.g., after a volcanic eruption or glacier retreat): pioneer species (lichens, mosses) colonise first → intermediate communities (grasses, herbs) → shrubs → climax community (stable, mature forest). Each stage modifies the environment, allowing the next community to develop.

questions.questionText: Scenario #11 — In a vaccination programme, which of the following correctly describes recombinant DNA technology? — in the mangrove swamp?

questions.explanation: Recombinant DNA technology: cutting DNA from two different organisms with restriction enzymes, joining them with DNA ligase, and inserting the recombinant DNA into a host cell (e.g., bacteria) to produce useful proteins (e.g., human insulin, growth hormone).

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a vaccination programme, which of the following correctly compares Darwin's and Lamarck's theories of evolution? — during a community survey?

options.label: A
options.text: Darwin's theory of natural selection states that organisms with favourable variations survive and reproduce; Lamarck's theory (now rejected) stated that acquired characteristics during life could be passed to offspring

options.label: B
options.text: Both Darwin and Lamarck proposed identical theories

options.label: C
options.text: Darwin's theory was based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics

options.label: D
options.text: Lamarck proposed natural selection; Darwin proposed inheritance of acquired characteristics

questions.explanation: Darwin's natural selection: individuals with favourable variations (arising randomly) survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest); over generations, the favourable trait accumulates in the population. Lamarck's (rejected) inheritance of acquired characteristics: features developed during life (e.g., giraffe's long neck from stretching) are passed to offspring.

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — In a vaccination programme, which of the following correctly describes codominance?

options.label: A
options.text: Codominance results in incomplete dominance (blending)

options.label: B
options.text: Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (e.g., ABO blood group AB, where both A and B antigens are present)

options.label: C
options.text: One allele completely masks the other

options.label: D
options.text: All codominant alleles produce recessive phenotypes

questions.explanation: Codominance: both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote (no dominant/recessive relationship). Example: ABO blood groups — IAIA = A, IBIB = B, IAIB = AB (both A and B antigens expressed). This is different from incomplete dominance, where traits blend.

questions.questionText: Scenario #14 — In a vaccination programme, what is meant by the term 'homeostasis' in human biology?

options.label: A
options.text: The maintenance of a stable internal environment (constant body temperature, pH, water balance and glucose level) despite external changes

options.label: B

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions to keep them stable despite external changes. Examples: thermoregulation (constant body temperature), osmoregulation (water balance), and blood glucose regulation (insulin + glucagon).

Discontinuous variation: discrete categories (one or few genes); examples: ABO blood group, tongue-rolling ability, seed shape, presence/absence of dimples.

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — During a family genetic counselling session, which of the following correctly describes the greenhouse effect? — context 47?

options.label: A
options.text: Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) trap heat in the Earth's atmosphere, leading to global warming and climate change

options.label: B
options.text: Greenhouse gases cool the Earth

options.label: C
options.text: Only CO₂ affects the climate

options.label: D
options.text: Greenhouse effect is caused by the ozone hole only

questions.explanation: Greenhouse effect: short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth's surface and is re-emitted as long-wave infrared (heat). Greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour) absorb and re-emit this heat, keeping Earth warm. Enhanced greenhouse effect (excess CO₂ from burning fossil fuels, deforestation) → global warming → climate change.

questions.questionText: Scenario #3 — During a family genetic counselling session, how does antibiotic resistance develop in bacterial populations?

options.label: A
options.text: All bacteria develop resistance after one exposure to antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: Resistance is caused by drinking antibiotics

options.label: C
options.text: Some bacteria have natural resistance; antibiotics kill susceptible ones; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring

options.label: D
options.text: Bacteria become resistant by becoming larger

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — During a family genetic counselling session, what are the sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms? — context 39?

options.label: A
options.text: Variation cannot be inherited

options.label: B
options.text: Variation is caused only by mutation

options.label: C
options.text: Genetic variation arises from sexual reproduction (crossing over, random assortment of chromosomes), random fertilisation and mutation

options.label: D
options.text: Variation is caused only by environment

questions.explanation: Genetic variation arises from three sources: (1) crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, (2) random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. Mutation creates new alleles. Environmental factors also contribute.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — During a family genetic counselling session, where is the hormone adrenaline produced in the human body?

options.label: A
options.text: Adrenal glands (situated above the kidneys)

options.label: B
options.text: Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)

options.label: C
options.text: Thyroid gland (in the neck)

options.label: D
options.text: Pituitary gland (at the base of the brain)

questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is produced by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of each kidney. It increases heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose in 'fight or flight' situations.

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — During a family genetic counselling session, which of the following correctly describes sex-linked inheritance?

options.label: A
options.text: All sex-linked traits affect females only

options.label: B
options.text: A carrier female (X^H X^h) crossed with a normal male (X^H Y) gives 1/4 affected male offspring

options.label: C
options.text: Sex-linked traits are carried on the Y chromosome only

options.label: D
options.text: Haemophilia is autosomal recessive

questions.explanation: Sex-linked traits (X-linked recessive) such as haemophilia and colour blindness: heterozygous females (X^H X^h) are carriers (phenotypically normal but carry one allele); males (X^h Y) express the trait. Cross X^H X^h × X^H Y → 1/4 X^h Y (affected male).

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — During a family genetic counselling session, in the menstrual cycle, what is ovulation?

options.label: C

questions.explanation: The release of a mature ovum (egg) from the ovary around day 14 — standard KSSM Form 5 reproductive biology.

questions.questionText: Scenario #9 — During a family genetic counselling session, which of the following correctly describes genetically modified (GM) food?

options.label: A
options.text: GM foods are always more nutritious

options.label: B
options.text: GM (genetically modified) foods contain genes from another species, introduced using recombinant DNA technology, to give desirable traits (e.g., pest resistance, longer shelf life)

options.label: C
options.text: GM foods are produced by selective breeding only

options.label: D
options.text: GM foods contain no DNA

questions.explanation: Genetically modified (GM) foods: contain one or more genes transferred from another species, conferring desirable traits (e.g., Bt corn with bacterial Bt gene for pest resistance; golden rice with added β-carotene for vitamin A). Controversies: unknown long-term health effects, environmental risks, ethical concerns.

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — During a family genetic counselling session, which of the following correctly distinguishes phenotype from genotype?

options.label: A
options.text: Genotype is the visible appearance

options.label: B
options.text: Phenotype is the allele composition

options.label: C
options.text: Phenotype and genotype are identical

options.label: D
options.text: Phenotype is the observable trait (e.g., tall plant); genotype is the genetic makeup (e.g., Tt)

questions.explanation: Phenotype: the observable characteristic (tall, short, red, etc.). Genotype: the genetic makeup (allele combination: e.g., TT, Tt, tt). Different genotypes can produce the same phenotype (e.g., TT and Tt both result in tall plants).

questions.questionText: Scenario #11 — During a family genetic counselling session, which of the following correctly defines a gene mutation?

options.label: A
options.text: Mutation is the gradual growth of an organism

options.label: B
options.text: Mutation is a sudden change in the DNA sequence that may be inherited

options.label: C
options.text: Mutation is the normal process of cell division

options.label: D
options.text: Mutation only occurs in muscle cells

questions.explanation: Mutation is a sudden, permanent change in the DNA sequence of a gene. Types: gene mutation (change in DNA base sequence) and chromosomal mutation (change in chromosome structure/number). Mutations can be inherited (if they occur in gametes) or cause genetic disorders.

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — During a family genetic counselling session, according to the 10% rule in ecosystems, what fraction of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?

options.label: A
options.text: Energy increases at higher trophic levels

options.label: B
options.text: Approximately 10% of energy is passed from one trophic level to the next; the rest is lost as heat, in undigested matter, or used in respiration

options.label: C
options.text: All energy passes to decomposers only

options.label: D
options.text: 100% of energy is transferred

questions.explanation: Energy flow in ecosystems: about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (10% rule). The rest is lost as heat (respiration), in undigested waste, or used for life processes. This is why food chains typically have only 4–5 trophic levels.

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — During a family genetic counselling session, which of the following correctly describes the 5-kingdom classification of living organisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Three kingdoms: animal, plant, fungi

options.label: B
options.text: Seven kingdoms (all sub-categories)

options.label: C
options.text: The 5-kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia

options.label: D
options.text: Two kingdoms: prokaryotes and eukaryotes only

questions.explanation: The 5-kingdom classification (Whittaker): Monera (prokaryotes: bacteria, cyanobacteria); Protista (protozoans, algae); Fungi (mushrooms, yeast); Plantae (plants); Animalia (animals).

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — In a genetics laboratory, which of the following correctly describes fermentation in biotechnology?

questions.explanation: Fermentation: anaerobic respiration by microorganisms (yeast, bacteria) to break down sugars. Examples: yeast fermentation → alcohol + CO₂ (bread-making, brewing); lactic acid bacteria fermentation → yogurt, cheese, kimchi; vinegar production by Acetobacter.

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions to keep them stable despite external changes. Examples: thermoregulation (constant body temperature), osmoregulation (water balance), and blood glucose regulation (insulin + glucagon).

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — In a genetics laboratory, how is the human blood glucose level regulated?

options.label: A
options.text: Insulin raises blood glucose

options.label: B
options.text: Blood glucose never changes during the day

options.label: C
options.text: When blood glucose rises, insulin is released to lower it; when blood glucose falls, glucagon is released to raise it

options.label: D
options.text: Hormones are produced in the adrenal glands only

questions.explanation: Blood glucose regulation uses negative feedback: a rise in blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion (lowering glucose), while a fall stimulates glucagon secretion (raising glucose). This keeps blood glucose within a narrow range (~4–7 mmol/L).

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — In a genetics laboratory, which of the following is an example of asexual reproduction? — context 47?

options.label: A
options.text: Sexual reproduction in humans

options.label: B
options.text: Binary fission in Amoeba

options.label: C
options.text: Cross-pollination in flowers

options.label: D
options.text: Fertilisation in mammals

questions.explanation: Binary fission in Amoeba. Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and produces offspring that are genetically identical (clones). Examples: binary fission (Amoeba, Paramecium), budding (Hydra, yeast), spore formation (Rhizopus, fern), and vegetative propagation (ginger, potato).

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — In a genetics laboratory, what is the difference between in-situ and ex-situ conservation?

options.label: A
options.text: Conservation refers only to animal species

options.label: B
options.text: In-situ conservation (e.g., national parks, wildlife reserves) protects species in their natural habitats; ex-situ conservation (e.g., zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks) protects species outside their natural habitats

options.label: C
options.text: Only ex-situ conservation is used in Malaysia

options.label: D
options.text: Both mean the same thing

questions.explanation: In-situ conservation: protecting species in their natural habitats (national parks like Taman Negara, wildlife reserves, marine parks). Ex-situ conservation: protecting species outside their natural habitats (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks, captive breeding programmes). Both are important for biodiversity.

questions.questionText: Scenario #9 — In a genetics laboratory, which of the following correctly describes cloning in biology?

options.label: A
options.text: Cloning produces genetically identical copies of an organism (asexual reproduction) or cell

options.label: B
options.text: Cloning always involves two parents

options.label: C
options.text: Cloning is impossible in mammals

options.label: D
options.text: Only plants can be cloned

questions.explanation: Cloning: producing genetically identical organisms from a single parent. Examples: asexual reproduction (binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation); somatic cell nuclear transfer (e.g., Dolly the sheep); tissue culture (plant cuttings in lab).

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — In a genetics laboratory, what is the correct order of trophic levels in a typical food chain?

options.label: A
options.text: Producer → Secondary consumer → Primary consumer

options.label: B
options.text: Producer (autotroph) → Primary consumer (herbivore) → Secondary consumer (carnivore) → Tertiary consumer → Decomposer

options.label: C
options.text: Decomposer → Producer → Consumer

options.label: D
options.text: Only producer and consumer exist

questions.explanation: Trophic levels in a food chain: Producers (green plants, photosynthetic) → Primary consumers (herbivores that eat plants) → Secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) → Tertiary consumers (top predators) → Decomposers (bacteria, fungi that break down dead matter).

questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus): each species is given a two-part Latin name. The first word (capitalised) is the genus; the second word (lower case) is the specific epithet. Both are italicised or underlined, e.g., Zea mays (corn).

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — In a genetics laboratory, a test cross is performed between a heterozygous parent (Aa) and a homozygous recessive (aa). What fraction of the offspring will be heterozygous?

options.label: A
options.text: 50% heterozygous (Aa) and 50% homozygous recessive (aa)

options.label: B
options.text: All offspring are heterozygous (Aa)

options.label: C
options.text: 75% homozygous dominant (AA)

options.label: D
options.text: 25% heterozygous (Aa) and 75% homozygous recessive (aa)

questions.explanation: Cross Aa × aa (test cross): parental gametes (A, a) × (a) → offspring Aa, Aa, aa, aa. Probability of heterozygous Aa = 1/2 (50%); probability of homozygous aa = 1/2 (50%).

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — In a genetics laboratory, which of the following correctly describes the process of natural selection as proposed by Darwin? — context 52?

options.label: A
options.text: Evolution happens only in bacteria

options.label: B
options.text: Offspring always inherit characteristics acquired during life

options.label: C
options.text: Variation in populations → struggle for existence → survival of the fittest → reproduction of the better-adapted organisms

options.label: D
options.text: All organisms survive equally well

questions.explanation: Natural selection (Darwin): (1) populations show variation; (2) there is a struggle for existence (competition for resources); (3) the best-adapted individuals survive and reproduce; (4) their favourable traits are passed to offspring; (5) over generations, the population becomes better adapted to its environment.

questions.questionText: Scenario #14 — In a genetics laboratory, which of the following describes how a nerve impulse is transmitted across a synapse?

options.label: A
options.text: A neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine) diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the next neurone

options.label: B
options.text: Two neurones fuse together permanently

options.label: C
options.text: Electric current flows directly from one neurone to another without any gap

options.label: D
options.text: Messages are transmitted only by sound waves

questions.explanation: Synapses are tiny gaps between two neurones. An electrical impulse arrives at the axon terminal, triggers release of neurotransmitter (e.g., acetylcholine), which diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the next neurone, generating a new impulse.

questions.questionText: Scenario #15 — In a genetics laboratory, which of the following correctly describes the female reproductive structure of a flower? — at the research centre?

options.label: A
options.text: Stigma (sticky, receives pollen) — Style (tube leading to ovary) — Ovary (contains ovules)

options.label: B
options.text: Sepal (sticky, receives pollen) — Receptacle (tube leading to ovary) — Anther (contains ovules)

options.label: C
options.text: Anther (sticky, receives pollen) — Filament (tube leading to ovary) — Petal (contains ovules)

options.label: D
options.text: Petal (sticky, receives pollen) — Sepal (tube leading to ovary) — Stamen (contains ovules)

questions.explanation: Female reproductive parts (pistil/carpel): stigma (sticky tip that receives pollen) — style (slender tube) — ovary (contains ovules). Male parts: anther (produces pollen) — filament.

questions.explanation: Genetic variation arises from three sources: (1) crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, (2) random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. questions.questionText: Scenario #2 — At an agricultural research station, which of the following correctly describes eutrophication in a freshwater lake?

options.label: A
options.text: Excess nitrates and phosphates (from fertilisers/sewage) cause algal blooms; algae die and decompose by aerobic bacteria, depleting oxygen and killing aquatic life

options.label: B
options.text: Eutrophication is caused by adding oxygen to lakes

options.label: C
options.text: Eutrophication means fish become larger

options.label: D
options.text: Eutrophication only happens in the ocean

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

questions.questionText: Scenario #3 — At an agricultural research station, which of the following correctly describes the inheritance of ABO blood groups?

options.label: A
options.text: ABO blood groups have nothing to do with alleles

options.label: B
options.text: All blood groups are controlled by two alleles only

options.label: C
options.text: ABO is controlled by a single dominant allele

options.label: D
options.text: ABO blood groups are determined by three alleles (I^A, I^B, i); I^A and I^B are codominant to each other and both are dominant over i

questions.explanation: ABO blood groups are a classic example of multiple alleles with codominance: three alleles (I^A, I^B, i) at one locus. I^A and I^B are codominant (expressed together in AB); both are dominant over i (recessive). Phenotypes: I^A I^A or I^A i = A; I^B I^B or I^B i = B; I^A I^B = AB; ii = O.

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — At an agricultural research station, in a Mendelian dihybrid cross of AaBb × AaBb, what is the expected phenotypic ratio among the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: Dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb (independent assortment) gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio — 9 dominant both : 3 dominant A, recessive b : 3 recessive a, dominant B : 1 recessive both.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — At an agricultural research station, what is the correct relationship between the dendrite and axon of a motor neurone?

options.label: A

questions.questionText: Scenario #8 — At an agricultural research station, what is the correct sequence of stages in ecological succession? — during a community survey?

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — At an agricultural research station, according to the 10% rule in ecosystems, what fraction of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions to keep them stable despite external changes. Examples: thermoregulation (constant body temperature), osmoregulation (water balance), and blood glucose regulation (insulin + glucagon).

options.text: Genetic variation arises from sexual reproduction (crossing over, random assortment of chromosomes), random fertilisation and mutation

options.text: Variation cannot be inherited

questions.explanation: Genetic variation arises from three sources: (1) crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, (2) random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. options.text: Eutrophication only happens in the ocean

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — In a school biology classroom, which of the following correctly compares Darwin's and Lamarck's theories of evolution?

options.text: Both Darwin and Lamarck proposed identical theories

options.text: Darwin's theory of natural selection states that organisms with favourable variations survive and reproduce; Lamarck's theory (now rejected) stated that acquired characteristics during life could be passed to offspring

questions.explanation: Darwin's natural selection: individuals with favourable variations (arising randomly) survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest); over generations, the favourable trait accumulates in the population. questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — At a botanical garden, which of the following correctly defines a gene mutation?

questions.questionText: Scenario #9 — In a fermentation factory, according to the 10% rule in ecosystems, what fraction of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next?

questions.explanation: Greenhouse effect: short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth's surface and is re-emitted as long-wave infrared (heat). Enhanced greenhouse effect (excess CO₂ from burning fossil fuels, deforestation) → global warming → climate change.

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — During a school nature camp, which of the following correctly describes binomial nomenclature?

questions.explanation: Binomial nomenclature (Carolus Linnaeus): each species is given a two-part Latin name. The first word (capitalised) is the genus; the second word (lower case) is the specific epithet. Both are italicised or underlined, e.g., Zea mays (corn).

questions.questionText: Scenario #6 — During a school nature camp, which of the following correctly describes eutrophication in a freshwater lake?

options.text: Excess nitrates and phosphates (from fertilisers/sewage) cause algal blooms; algae die and decompose by aerobic bacteria, depleting oxygen and killing aquatic life

questions.explanation: Eutrophication: fertiliser run-off (nitrates/phosphates) or sewage discharge into a lake/river causes excessive algal growth (algal bloom). When the algae die, decomposers (aerobic bacteria) break them down, consuming dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic life suffocate.

questions.questionText: Scenario #7 — During a school nature camp, how is the human blood glucose level regulated?

questions.explanation: Blood glucose regulation uses negative feedback: a rise in blood glucose stimulates insulin secretion (lowering glucose), while a fall stimulates glucagon secretion (raising glucose). This keeps blood glucose within a narrow range (~4–7 mmol/L).

questions.questionText: Scenario #9 — During a school nature camp, what are the sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms? — context 24?

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — During a school nature camp, what is the correct sequence of stages in ecological succession?

questions.explanation: Energy flow in ecosystems: about 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next (10% rule). The rest is lost as heat (respiration), in undigested waste, or used for life processes. This is why food chains typically have only 4–5 trophic levels.

Each stage modifies the environment, allowing the next community to develop.

questions.questionText: Scenario #9 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly defines a gene mutation? — context 85?

options.label: A
options.text: Mutation only occurs in muscle cells

options.label: B
options.text: Mutation is a sudden change in the DNA sequence that may be inherited

options.label: C
options.text: Mutation is the normal process of cell division

options.label: D
options.text: Mutation is the gradual growth of an organism

questions.explanation: Mutation is a sudden, permanent change in the DNA sequence of a gene. Types: gene mutation (change in DNA base sequence) and chromosomal mutation (change in chromosome structure/number). Mutations can be inherited (if they occur in gametes) or cause genetic disorders.

questions.questionText: Scenario #10 — During a secondary-school biology lab, asexual reproduction involves?

options.label: A
options.text: Only one parent; offspring are genetically identical to the parent

options.label: B
options.text: Cross-pollination

options.label: C
options.text: Two parents; offspring are genetically different from parents

options.label: D
options.text: Gamete formation and fertilisation

questions.explanation: Only one parent; offspring are genetically identical to the parent. Asexual reproduction involves a single parent and produces offspring that are genetically identical (clones). Examples: binary fission (Amoeba, Paramecium), budding (Hydra, yeast), spore formation (Rhizopus, fern), and vegetative propagation (ginger, potato).

questions.questionText: Scenario #11 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes genetically modified (GM) food?

options.label: A
options.text: GM foods are always more nutritious

options.label: B
options.text: GM foods are produced by selective breeding only

options.label: C
options.text: GM foods contain no DNA

options.label: D
options.text: GM (genetically modified) foods contain genes from another species, introduced using recombinant DNA technology, to give desirable traits (e.g., pest resistance, longer shelf life)

questions.explanation: Genetically modified (GM) foods: contain one or more genes transferred from another species, conferring desirable traits (e.g., Bt corn with bacterial Bt gene for pest resistance; golden rice with added β-carotene for vitamin A). Controversies: unknown long-term health effects, environmental risks, ethical concerns.

questions.questionText: Scenario #12 — During a secondary-school biology lab, what is the correct order of trophic levels in a typical food chain?

options.label: A
options.text: Producer → Secondary consumer → Primary consumer

options.label: B
options.text: Producer (autotroph) → Primary consumer (herbivore) → Secondary consumer (carnivore) → Tertiary consumer → Decomposer

options.label: C
options.text: Decomposer → Producer → Consumer

options.label: D
options.text: Only producer and consumer exist

questions.explanation: Trophic levels in a food chain: Producers (green plants, photosynthetic) → Primary consumers (herbivores that eat plants) → Secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) → Tertiary consumers (top predators) → Decomposers (bacteria, fungi that break down dead matter).

questions.questionText: Scenario #13 — During a secondary-school biology lab, what are the sources of genetic variation in sexually reproducing organisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Variation is caused only by environment

options.label: B
options.text: Variation cannot be inherited

options.label: C
options.text: Variation is caused only by mutation

options.label: D
options.text: Genetic variation arises from sexual reproduction (crossing over, random assortment of chromosomes), random fertilisation and mutation

questions.explanation: Genetic variation arises from three sources: (1) crossing over between homologous chromosomes during meiosis, (2) random assortment of chromosomes during meiosis, (3) random fusion of gametes at fertilisation. Mutation creates new alleles. Environmental factors also contribute.

questions.questionText: Scenario #14 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes the divisions of the human nervous system?

options.label: A
options.text: Stomach and intestines

options.label: B
options.text: Heart and blood vessels

options.label: C
options.text: Lungs and liver

options.label: D
options.text: Central nervous system (brain + spinal cord) and peripheral nervous system

questions.explanation: The human nervous system is divided into: (1) Central Nervous System (CNS) — brain and spinal cord, which integrate and process information; (2) Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) — nerves that connect the CNS to the rest of the body.

questions.questionText: Scenario #15 — During a secondary-school biology lab, which of the following correctly describes sex-linked inheritance?

options.label: A
options.text: Sex-linked traits are carried on the Y chromosome only

options.label: B
options.text: Haemophilia is autosomal recessive

options.label: C
options.text: A carrier female (X^H X^h) crossed with a normal male (X^H Y) gives 1/4 affected male offspring

options.label: D
options.text: All sex-linked traits affect females only

questions.explanation: Sex-linked traits (X-linked recessive) such as haemophilia and colour blindness: heterozygous females (X^H X^h) are carriers (phenotypically normal but carry one allele); males (X^h Y) express the trait. Cross X^H X^h × X^H Y → 1/4 X^h Y (affected male).

questions.questionText: Scenario #1 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly describes the 5-kingdom classification of living organisms?

options.label: A
options.text: Two kingdoms: prokaryotes and eukaryotes only

options.label: B
options.text: Three kingdoms: animal, plant, fungi

options.label: C
options.text: Seven kingdoms (all sub-categories)

options.label: D
options.text: The 5-kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia

questions.explanation: The 5-kingdom classification (Whittaker): Monera (prokaryotes: bacteria, cyanobacteria); Protista (protozoans, algae); Fungi (mushrooms, yeast); Plantae (plants); Animalia (animals).

questions.questionText: Scenario #2 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, how does antibiotic resistance develop in bacterial populations?

options.label: A
options.text: All bacteria develop resistance after one exposure to antibiotics

options.label: B
options.text: Some bacteria have natural resistance; antibiotics kill susceptible ones; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring

options.label: C
options.text: Resistance is caused by drinking antibiotics

options.label: D
options.text: Bacteria become resistant by becoming larger

questions.explanation: Antibiotic resistance arises by natural selection: in a population, some bacteria carry resistance alleles (random mutation). When exposed to the antibiotic, susceptible bacteria die while resistant bacteria survive and multiply, increasing the frequency of resistance genes.

questions.questionText: Scenario #3 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, in a Mendelian dihybrid cross of AaBb × AaBb, what is the expected phenotypic ratio among the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: Dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb (independent assortment) gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio — 9 dominant both : 3 dominant A, recessive b : 3 recessive a, dominant B : 1 recessive both.

questions.questionText: Scenario #4 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, where is the hormone adrenaline produced in the human body?

options.label: A
options.text: Thyroid gland (in the neck)

options.label: B
options.text: Adrenal glands (situated above the kidneys)

options.label: C
options.text: Pituitary gland (at the base of the brain)

options.label: D
options.text: Pancreas (islets of Langerhans)

questions.explanation: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is produced by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of each kidney. It increases heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose in 'fight or flight' situations.

questions.questionText: Scenario #5 — In a tropical rainforest field trip, which of the following correctly distinguishes phenotype from genotype?

options.label: A
options.text: Phenotype and genotype are identical

options.label: B
options.text: Phenotype is the allele composition

options.label: C
options.text: Genotype is the visible appearance

options.label: D
options.text: Phenotype is the observable trait (e.g., tall plant); genotype is the genetic makeup (e.g., Tt)

questions.explanation: Phenotype: the observable characteristic (tall, short, red, etc.). Genotype: the genetic makeup (allele combination: e.g., TT, Tt, tt). Different genotypes can produce the same phenotype (e.g., TT and Tt both result in tall plants).
